newsitem.title: USA: U.S. attorney general criticizes Saudi bomb probe.
newsitem.headline: U.S. attorney general criticizes Saudi bomb probe.

text.p: Attorney General Janet Reno on Thursday joined FBI chief Louis Freeh in complaining that Saudi Arabia has failed to turn over key information about the truck bombing that killed 19 U.S. servicemen last year.

"As Director Freeh said yesterday, the Saudi government has not furnished us with some very important information," Reno told her weekly Justice Department news briefing. "I am hopeful that we will be able to address these issues (and) obtain the information so appropriate steps can be taken."

FBI officials privately have long complained about a lack of cooperation from Saudi authorities in investigating the June 25 bombing at a U.S. military housing complex in Dhahran. They said FBI agents were not allowed to question Saudi citizens and were not told about arrests, and that Saudi authorities refused to share all their evidence with them.

But publicly top FBI officials had sought to praise Saudi cooperation until Freeh charged at a Wednesday meeting at the Washington Post that Saudi Arabia had frustrated U.S. efforts to determine responsibility for the attack. An FBI spokesman said Freeh stood by his remarks.

Freeh said he did not have enough information to make "strong findings or conclusions" because what he had been told was "hearsay information in many cases." He added, "There is a great deal of information that we have not seen.
Reno, who oversees the FBI, agreed with Freeh. "I think it's important in any investigation to have full information in order to assess what action should be taken."
She declined to discuss specific information Saudi Arabia had refused to provide, saying it would be inappropriate to go into detail. "That is a pending investigation," she said.

Reno said the Justice Department would work with the State Department, the White House National Security Council and the FBI "to coordinate" with the Saudi government. She declined comment when asked whether the evidence might show Iran's complicity in the bombing.

The Washington Post reported last year that Saudi authorities were convinced Iran had backed a broad conspiracy in the attack. Iran has rejected the charges and top Clinton administration officials have said the United States has not yet concluded who was responsible for the bombing.

Freeh in November made his third trip to Saudi Arabia for discussions about the investigation, saying at the time the United States supported Saudi efforts to solve the crime. But Justice Department officials privately have expressed little hope that any suspects would ever be turned over for prosecution in the United States.
